patient.name: Grace Mensah
patient.complaint: Daily cough with large amounts of green sputum for two years
background: Pulmonary TB in 2011, completed 6 months of treatment
Never smoked; school administrator in Hackney

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with a chronic productive cough of copious purulent sputum, a past serious infection (pneumonia, TB) or CF, coarse crackles and clubbing. Also 'most likely cause' or 'most likely organism'.

points: Coughs up **a cupful of green sputum** every day for two years.
Sometimes the sputum has **red specks** in it.
Four courses of antibiotics this year; each helps briefly.

steps.lead: A daily, years-long cough with pots of purulent sputum means the airways themselves are damaged: Grace's bronchi are **permanently dilated** and cannot clear mucus.
Grace has the **most important** cause twice over: childhood pneumonia and previous **TB**.

points: **Coarse inspiratory crackles** at both bases, some wheeze.
Crackles change after she coughs up sputum.
No weight loss, no night sweats.

steps.lead: Grace has the full picture: copious **'green sputum with red specks'**, inspiratory crackles, wheeze and clubbing.

steps.q: Grace has never smoked, coughs up copious green sputum daily and had TB. What is most likely?
steps.r: Copious purulent sputum for years after a serious infection is **bronchiectasis**. COPD needs smoking; IPF gives a dry cough with fine velcro crackles.

steps.title: Chronic cough: how to tell them apart
head: Feature
Bronchiectasis
COPD
IPF
TB reactivation

steps.lead: Grace is 56 with no gut or diabetes symptoms, so not CF. A **young** patient with clubbing, haemoptysis and pancreatic failure would be the CF picture.
Each of Grace's four infections this year probably came from **Haemophilus influenzae**, and every one adds more damage.

steps.text: Clubbing is **not** a feature of COPD. A 'COPD' stem with clubbing should make you think bronchiectasis, fibrosis or lung cancer.
Asthma + bronchiectasis + very high **eosinophils** = **ABPA** as the cause. Young + pancreatic problems = **CF**. Dextrocardia + sinusitis + subfertility = **primary ciliary dyskinesia**.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate investigation to establish the diagnosis?' (HRCT chest), plus sputum culture to guide antibiotics and tests for the cause (immunoglobulins, CF testing).

steps.q: Which test will confirm Grace's diagnosis?
steps.r: **HRCT** is the gold standard and shows the dilated airways. A chest X-ray is often normal or non-specific.

steps.lead: Grace's HRCT shows dilated, thick-walled bronchi in both lower lobes: **signet ring** and **tram-track** signs.

steps.title: HRCT signs of bronchiectasis
head: Sign
What you see
Why
rows: String of pearls / cluster of grapes

steps.lead: Grace's sputum is sent for **culture** so the next antibiotic is chosen by the organism, not guessed.

steps.title: Sputum culture (clinic)
steps.text: The commonest organism. Pseudomonas would change her antibiotics and prognosis.

visual.title: Grace's FEV1/FVC ratio
visual.label: Grace 0.63
visual.caption: FEV1/FVC below 0.7: an obstructive pattern, as in bronchiectasis.

steps.lead: Grace's spirometry is **obstructive** (FEV1/FVC 0.63), the expected pattern; it tracks severity over time.
Grace's cause looks post-infective, but she still has **immunoglobulins** checked. CF testing is for younger patients or suggestive features.

steps.text: Do not pick **chest X-ray** or **spirometry** for 'establish the diagnosis'. Only HRCT shows the dilated bronchi.

management.exam: Expect 'most appropriate initial management' (chest physiotherapy), 'which antibiotic' for an exacerbation, and 'next step' when exacerbations reach 3 or more a year or disease is confined to one lobe.

steps.q: What is the first-line long-term treatment for Grace's stable bronchiectasis?
steps.r: **Chest physiotherapy** (airway clearance) is first-line. Steroids are for ABPA, not routine bronchiectasis.

steps.lead: Grace learns **airway clearance** with a physiotherapist: postural drainage and breathing techniques twice a day, with **hypertonic saline** nebs to loosen sputum.

points: Six months later: sputum more purulent, more breathless.
No high fever; breathing comfortably at home.

steps.lead: Grace is well enough for the community: **14 days of oral ciprofloxacin**, which also covers her Pseudomonas. A high fever and raised RR would mean IV.

visual.title: Exacerbations in the last 12 months
visual.label: Grace 5
visual.caption: Five exacerbations despite good airway clearance: prophylactic antibiotics are indicated.

steps.lead: Grace now has **3 or more exacerbations a year** with Pseudomonas, so she starts an **inhaled aminoglycoside**, plus vaccines and a bronchodilator.
Grace's disease is in **both** lower lobes, so surgery is not an option. If HRCT showed **one lobe** only, resection could cure it.
Grace is told: coughing up **large amounts of fresh blood** is an emergency; call 999.

steps.title: Bronchiectasis management ladder
nodes: Exacerbation: sputum culture, 14 days of antibiotics
Unwell (high fever, raised RR) → IV antibiotics
≥3 exacerbations/year → prophylactic macrolide or inhaled aminoglycoside
One lobe only on HRCT → consider surgery
steps.caption: Physiotherapy underpins every step.

steps.lead: Grace's care hits both guideline points: HRCT confirmed the diagnosis, and her 5 exacerbations cross the **≥3 per year** threshold.

steps.text: Inhaled corticosteroids are not routine in bronchiectasis. Steroids are the answer only when the cause is **ABPA**.

science.exam: Expect applied questions: why the wall dilates permanently (proteases destroying elastin and cartilage), why the same organisms keep coming back, or how CFTR causes thick mucus.

steps.title: The vicious cycle
steps.caption: Each turn of the cycle makes the next infection more likely.

steps.lead: Grace's childhood pneumonia started a cycle of **infection, inflammation and poor clearance** that kept going long after the first infection cleared.
The dilatation in Grace's airways is **irreversible** because proteases have digested the elastin and cartilage that hold the bronchi in shape.
Grace's pooled mucus is a permanent home for bacteria, which is why **H. influenzae** and then **Pseudomonas** keep coming back.

steps.q: In cystic fibrosis, what directly makes the airway mucus so hard to clear?
steps.r: A defective **CFTR** channel means less chloride and water reach the airway surface, so mucus is thick and dehydrated.

steps.lead: Grace does not have CF, but in CF the faulty **CFTR** channel leaves mucus thick and dry from birth, so bronchiectasis starts young.

visual.title: Grace's FEV1 over time
visual.caption: Recurrent exacerbations drive a steady fall; slowing it is the aim of treatment.

mcq.q: What is the most common cause of bronchiectasis?
mcq.r: **Previous infection** is the most important cause; CF is the classic cause in the young.

mcq.q: Which organism most commonly causes bronchiectasis exacerbations?
mcq.r: **Haemophilus influenzae** is the most common. Pseudomonas is important but less common.

mcq.q: Which sputum description is classic for bronchiectasis?
mcq.r: Copious purulent **'green sputum with red specks'**.

mcq.q: What is the gold-standard investigation for bronchiectasis?
mcq.r: **HRCT** shows signet ring, tram-track and string of pearls signs.

mcq.q: What spirometry pattern is seen in bronchiectasis?
What is the first-line management of bronchiectasis?
Which regimen do the notes give for a community exacerbation?
mcq.r: **14 days of oral ciprofloxacin**; IV if high fever and raised RR.
**3 or more exacerbations a year** despite optimal management.

mcq.q: Why is the bronchial dilatation irreversible?
mcq.r: Inflammatory **proteases** destroy the elastin and cartilage of the bronchial wall.

prompts.q: What is bronchiectasis and what are its causes?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the cause is often the hidden clue in the stem.

points.p: Permanent (irreversible) dilatation of the bronchi
points.why: Permanent is what separates it from simple bronchitis.

points.p: Impaired mucus clearance and recurrent infection
points.why: Mucus pooling drives the recurrent infections.

points.p: Most important cause: previous infection (pneumonia, TB)
points.why: Look for childhood pneumonia, whooping cough, measles or TB in the stem.

points.p: Cystic fibrosis and primary ciliary dyskinesia
Immunodeficiency, ABPA and rheumatoid arthritis
points.why: ABPA: asthma plus very high eosinophils.

prompts.q: How does bronchiectasis present, and what do you find on examination?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: copious purulent sputum is the word that should trigger it.

points.p: Persistent productive cough with copious purulent sputum
points.why: Daily, large volumes, for months to years.

points.p: Green sputum with red specks (haemoptysis)
Coarse inspiratory crackles and wheeze
points.why: Fine velcro crackles point to fibrosis instead.

points.p: Finger clubbing in advanced disease

prompts.q: Describe the classic CF-related bronchiectasis patient.
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: young patient + lung + pancreas = CF.

points.p: Young patient
Productive cough, haemoptysis and clubbing
points.why: Same lung picture as other causes.

points.p: Bilateral coarse crepitations
points.why: Diffuse disease, unlike localised post-infective damage.

points.p: Pancreatic dysfunction, exocrine and endocrine
points.why: Steatorrhoea and CF-related diabetes are the giveaways.

prompts.q: What is the most common exacerbation organism, and what do exacerbations do?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: 'most likely organism' in bronchiectasis is H. influenzae unless Pseudomonas is stated.

points.p: Haemophilus influenzae is the most common
points.why: Pseudomonas colonisation marks more severe disease.

points.p: Recurrent exacerbations drive progressive lung damage
points.why: Hence prophylaxis at 3 or more a year.

points.p: Massive haemoptysis is a complication and an emergency

prompts.q: Which clue points to each specific cause: ABPA, CF, PCD, immunodeficiency?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the 'most likely cause' question hides one extra clue.

points.p: ABPA: asthma with very high eosinophils
CF: young, steatorrhoea or diabetes
points.why: Confirm with a sweat test or genetics.

points.p: PCD: dextrocardia, sinusitis, subfertility
points.why: Kartagener syndrome is PCD with situs inversus.

points.p: Immunodeficiency: recurrent sinus and other infections, low immunoglobulins

prompts.q: What is the gold-standard investigation, and what three signs does it show?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: 'establish the diagnosis' = HRCT, not X-ray or spirometry.

points.p: High-resolution CT (HRCT) chest
Signet ring sign
points.why: Bronchus wider than its accompanying artery.

points.p: Tram-track sign
points.why: Thick parallel bronchial walls seen lengthways.

points.p: String of pearls / cluster of grapes

prompts.q: Which other tests do you send, and what do they show?

points.p: Sputum culture to identify the organism and guide antibiotics
Spirometry: obstructive pattern (FEV1/FVC below 0.7)
Serum immunoglobulins
CF testing (sweat test, genetics) if suspected

prompts.q: What is first-line treatment, and how is an exacerbation treated?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: physio for stable disease; 14 days of antibiotics for an exacerbation.

points.p: Chest physiotherapy: postural drainage, airway clearance, inspiratory muscle training
Inhaled hypertonic saline as an adjunct
Community exacerbation: 14 days of oral ciprofloxacin
points.why: Bronchiectasis courses are 14 days, longer than for pneumonia.

points.p: IV antibiotics if high fever and raised RR
ABPA: corticosteroids
points.why: The only routine steroid indication here.

prompts.q: What is the next step after repeated exacerbations, for localised disease, and for massive haemoptysis?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: know the number 3 and the phrase 'one lobe'.

points.p: ≥3 exacerbations a year despite optimal care: prophylactic antibiotics
Oral macrolide (azithromycin) or inhaled aminoglycoside if Pseudomonas
Bronchodilators and vaccination as support
Surgery if HRCT shows disease confined to one lobe
Massive haemoptysis is a medical emergency

prompts.q: Why does bronchiectasis keep progressing, and why is it irreversible?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the vicious cycle and proteases.

points.p: Cycle of infection, inflammation and impaired mucociliary clearance
Proteases and mediators digest elastin and cartilage
points.why: Loss of wall support = permanent dilatation.

points.p: Pooled mucus gives a nidus for chronic colonisation (H. influenzae, Pseudomonas)

prompts.q: Why does cystic fibrosis cause bronchiectasis?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: name the channel and the effect on mucus.

points.p: Defective CFTR chloride channel
points.why: Autosomal recessive; delta F508 is the commonest mutation.

points.p: Thick, dehydrated mucus that cannot be cleared
points.why: Less chloride and water on the airway surface.

points.p: Predisposes to chronic infection
points.why: Pseudomonas and Staph aureus are classic in CF.

glossary.Bronchiectasis: Permanent dilatation of the bronchi with poor mucus clearance and recurrent infection.
glossary.HRCT: High-resolution CT: thin-slice CT of the lungs, the gold standard for bronchiectasis and fibrosis.
glossary.Signet ring sign: On HRCT, a dilated bronchus next to its smaller artery, like a ring with a stone.
glossary.Tram-track sign: Parallel thickened bronchial walls seen lengthways on imaging.
glossary.String of pearls: Beaded, varicose dilatation of bronchi on HRCT.
glossary.Cluster of grapes: Groups of cystic dilated bronchi on HRCT in severe bronchiectasis.
glossary.Clubbing: Loss of the nail-bed angle and bulbous fingertips, seen in chronic suppurative lung disease and fibrosis.
glossary.Crepitations: Crackles heard with a stethoscope; coarse in bronchiectasis, fine in fibrosis.
glossary.Purulent: Containing pus; green or yellow sputum.
glossary.Exacerbation: An acute worsening of symptoms, usually from infection.
glossary.Haemophilus influenzae: Gram-negative coccobacillus; the commonest organism in bronchiectasis exacerbations.
glossary.Pseudomonas aeruginosa: Gram-negative rod that chronically colonises damaged airways; marks more severe disease.
glossary.Cystic fibrosis: Autosomal recessive CFTR defect causing thick secretions in lungs, pancreas and gut.
glossary.CFTR: Cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator, an epithelial chloride channel.
glossary.Primary ciliary dyskinesia: Inherited defect of cilia causing poor mucus clearance, sinusitis, subfertility and sometimes dextrocardia.
glossary.Kartagener syndrome: Primary ciliary dyskinesia with situs inversus.
glossary.ABPA: Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis: hypersensitivity to Aspergillus in asthma or CF, causing central bronchiectasis.
glossary.Mucociliary clearance: The cilia-driven escalator that moves mucus and trapped particles out of the airways.
glossary.Postural drainage: Positioning so gravity drains sputum from affected lung segments.
glossary.Airway clearance techniques: Physiotherapy breathing methods that help shift and cough up sputum.
glossary.Hypertonic saline: Concentrated salt solution, nebulised to draw water into mucus and loosen it.
glossary.Ciprofloxacin: Oral fluoroquinolone antibiotic that covers Pseudomonas.
glossary.Macrolide: Antibiotic class including azithromycin and clarithromycin; long-term use reduces exacerbations.
glossary.Azithromycin: Macrolide used long term to prevent bronchiectasis exacerbations.
glossary.Aminoglycoside: Antibiotic class (e.g. tobramycin, gentamicin); inhaled forms suppress Pseudomonas.
glossary.FEV1/FVC: Fraction of the vital capacity breathed out in one second; below 0.7 means obstruction.
glossary.Obstructive pattern: Spirometry with FEV1/FVC below 0.7, from narrowed or collapsing airways.
glossary.Immunoglobulins: Antibodies (IgG, IgA, IgM); low levels suggest immunodeficiency as a cause.
glossary.Elastin: Stretchy protein in the bronchial wall that holds it in shape.
glossary.Proteases: Enzymes, for example neutrophil elastase, that break down proteins in tissue.
glossary.Nidus: A focus where infection settles and persists.
glossary.Sweat test: Measures sweat chloride; raised in cystic fibrosis.
glossary.Dextrocardia: Heart on the right side of the chest.

technique.stem: A 49 year old man has a 3 year history of a daily cough productive of large volumes of green sputum, sometimes with red specks. He had pulmonary tuberculosis 15 years ago, which was fully treated. He has never smoked. He has had five courses of antibiotics this year. There are coarse inspiratory crackles at both bases and his fingers are clubbed.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: A diagnosis question about a chronic cough: the sputum and the history decide it.
Copious purulent sputum for years after a serious infection, coarse crackles and clubbing.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Post-infective (post-TB) **bronchiectasis**.

elim: COPD needs smoking and does not cause clubbing.
Lung cancer gives weight loss and a new cough, not 3 years of copious sputum.
TB was fully treated; no fevers, sweats or weight loss now.
Sarcoidosis gives a dry cough, BHL and skin or eye signs.

steps.x: **A. Bronchiectasis.** Rule: copious purulent sputum + past infection + clubbing = bronchiectasis.

technique.stem: A 33 year old woman has had recurrent chest infections since childhood whooping cough. She coughs up purulent sputum most days. Her temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 80 bpm, BP 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 97% breathing air. Her chest X-ray is reported as normal.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to establish the diagnosis?

steps.x: 'Establish the diagnosis' means the gold-standard test.

clues: recurrent chest infections since childhood whooping cough
chest X-ray is reported as normal
steps.x: Classic post-infective bronchiectasis story; a normal CXR does not exclude it.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **HRCT chest** shows the dilated bronchi (signet ring, tram-track).

elim: Bronchoscopy is for masses, foreign bodies or lavage, not to diagnose bronchiectasis.
Repeating a CXR will not show the airway dilatation.
Cultures guide antibiotics; they do not make the diagnosis.
Spirometry shows obstruction but is not specific.

steps.x: **C. High-resolution CT chest.** Rule: bronchiectasis is confirmed on HRCT.

technique.stem: A 41 year old woman has bronchiectasis following a severe right lower lobe pneumonia in her twenties. She has three or four exacerbations a year despite daily airway clearance physiotherapy. HRCT shows bronchiectasis confined to the right lower lobe, with the rest of both lungs normal. Her FEV1 is 82% of predicted.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate definitive management?
o: Surgical resection of the right lower lobe

steps.x: 'Definitive' asks what can remove the disease, not just control it.

clues: confined to the right lower lobe
steps.x: Localised disease, good lung function, failing conservative care.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Disease in **one lobe** on HRCT: **surgical resection**.

elim: Physio alone is already failing.
Inhaled steroids are not a bronchiectasis treatment unless ABPA.
Azithromycin prevents exacerbations but does not remove the disease.
Transplant is for end-stage diffuse disease, not one lobe.

steps.x: **E. Surgical resection.** Rule: one lobe on HRCT = consider surgery.

technique.stem: A 17 year old boy has a productive cough, recurrent chest infections and finger clubbing. He has frequent pale, greasy stools that are hard to flush and he is underweight. HRCT shows widespread bilateral bronchiectasis. A sweat chloride test is raised.
technique.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his bronchiectasis?

steps.x: A mechanism question: first name the cause, then the mechanism.
Young, steatorrhoea (exocrine pancreas) and a raised sweat chloride: **cystic fibrosis**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: CF: **defective CFTR** causes thick, dehydrated mucus that cannot be cleared.

elim: A1AT deficiency gives basal emphysema and liver disease.
Dynein defects cause PCD, with a normal sweat test.
IgG deficiency causes infections but not steatorrhoea or a raised sweat chloride.
ABPA occurs in asthma with eosinophilia.

steps.x: **B. Defective CFTR chloride channel.** Rule: young + lungs + pancreas + sweat test = CF.

practice.stem: A 52 year old man has a 2 year history of a cough producing about a cupful of purulent sputum each day. He had a severe pneumonia as a child. He has never smoked. His temperature is 37.0°C, pulse rate 82 bpm, BP 132/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 96% breathing air. He has coarse crackles at both bases and finger clubbing.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Daily copious purulent sputum after childhood pneumonia, coarse crackles and clubbing is bronchiectasis. IPF gives a dry cough with fine velcro crackles; COPD needs smoking.

steps.x: Diagnosis of a chronic productive cough.

clues: cupful of purulent sputum each day
steps.x: Copious sputum, past infection, coarse crackles, clubbing.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Bronchiectasis**, post-infective.

elim: No smoking history, and COPD does not club.
IPF: dry cough, fine end-inspiratory crackles.
No weight loss or haemoptysis; 2 years of copious sputum fits better.
No fevers, sweats or weight loss.

steps.x: **A. Bronchiectasis.**

practice.stem: A 19 year old man has bronchiectasis confirmed on HRCT. He has had a productive cough since childhood, with occasional haemoptysis. He has finger clubbing, bilateral coarse crepitations and is underweight. He has frequent loose, pale, offensive stools.
practice.q: Which is the most likely underlying cause?
practice.e: A young patient with bronchiectasis plus exocrine (low faecal elastase, steatorrhoea) and endocrine (raised HbA1c) pancreatic failure has cystic fibrosis. PCD does not affect the pancreas.

steps.x: He has bronchiectasis; you need the **cause**.
Young, lifelong, diffuse disease, steatorrhoea; labs show low faecal elastase and raised HbA1c.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Lungs + exocrine + endocrine pancreas = **cystic fibrosis**.

elim: ABPA needs asthma and eosinophilia.
PCD gives sinusitis and subfertility, not pancreatic failure.
No TB history, and TB does not affect the pancreas.
RA is a cause in older adults with joint disease.

steps.x: **B. Cystic fibrosis.**

practice.stem: A 63 year old woman with bronchiectasis has 4 days of increased volume and purulence of her sputum. She has no previous sputum culture results. Her temperature is 37.8°C, pulse rate 94 bpm, BP 126/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 95% breathing air.
practice.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
practice.e: Haemophilus influenzae is the most common organism in bronchiectasis exacerbations. Pseudomonas matters but is less common and usually known from previous cultures.

steps.x: Most likely organism in a bronchiectasis exacerbation.
An infective exacerbation with no known colonisation.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Haemophilus influenzae**.

elim: Aspergillus causes ABPA, not routine exacerbations.
Moraxella is more a COPD exacerbation organism.
Pseudomonas is important but less common; no previous culture suggests it.
Pneumococcus is the commonest cause of CAP, not bronchiectasis exacerbations.

steps.x: **B. Haemophilus influenzae.**

practice.stem: A 58 year old woman has had a daily cough with purulent sputum since a severe pneumonia ten years ago. HRCT shows dilated, thick-walled bronchi in both lower lobes. She has never smoked. She has spirometry in clinic.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on spirometry?
o: Reversibility of more than 400 mL after salbutamol
practice.e: Bronchiectasis gives an obstructive pattern (FEV1/FVC below 0.7). A restrictive pattern with a preserved ratio is fibrosis; large reversibility is asthma.

steps.x: A finding question: what does spirometry show in this condition?

clues: purulent sputum since a severe pneumonia
steps.x: Post-infective bronchiectasis confirmed on HRCT.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Bronchiectasis is an airway disease: **obstructive**, FEV1/FVC below 0.7.

elim: A mixed pattern is not the expected finding.
Established symptomatic bronchiectasis usually shows obstruction.
Restrictive with a preserved ratio is fibrosis.
Marked reversibility is asthma.

steps.x: **C. Obstructive pattern.**

practice.stem: A 28 year old man has bronchiectasis on HRCT. He has had a wet cough and recurrent sinusitis since early childhood. He and his partner have been unable to conceive for 3 years and his semen shows immotile sperm. His heart sounds are loudest on the right side of his chest.
practice.q: Which is the most likely underlying cause?
practice.e: Bronchiectasis, chronic sinusitis, immotile sperm and dextrocardia is primary ciliary dyskinesia (Kartagener syndrome). CF causes male infertility through absent vas deferens, not immotile sperm, and gives pancreatic disease.

steps.x: Cause of bronchiectasis.

clues: heart sounds are loudest on the right side
steps.x: Cilia and sperm tails share the same dynein machinery; dextrocardia = situs inversus.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Primary ciliary dyskinesia** (Kartagener).

elim: ABPA needs asthma and eosinophilia.
CVID causes infections but not immotile sperm or dextrocardia.
CF infertility is from absent vas deferens, with pancreatic disease.
No TB history.

steps.x: **E. Primary ciliary dyskinesia.**

practice.stem: A 66 year old woman has had a cough with copious purulent sputum for 4 years. She had pulmonary tuberculosis in her thirties. Her temperature is 36.9°C, pulse rate 78 bpm, BP 138/82 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 96% breathing air.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on auscultation of her chest?
o: Bronchial breathing over the right upper zone
Fine end-inspiratory crackles that do not change with coughing
practice.e: Bronchiectasis gives coarse inspiratory crackles (often changing with coughing as sputum moves). Fine velcro crackles are fibrosis; bronchial breathing is consolidation.

steps.x: A finding question: first make the diagnosis, then pick its sign.
Post-TB bronchiectasis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Sputum in dilated airways: **coarse inspiratory crackles**.

elim: Bronchial breathing is consolidation.
Fine velcro crackles are pulmonary fibrosis.
A pleural rub is pleurisy or PE.
A silent chest is life-threatening asthma.

steps.x: **B. Coarse inspiratory crackles.**

practice.stem: A 60 year old man with known bronchiectasis has 3 days of increased, more purulent sputum. He is not systemically unwell. His temperature is 37.4°C, pulse rate 88 bpm, BP 134/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 17 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 96% breathing air. His GP plans to start oral antibiotics today.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation before starting antibiotics?
practice.e: Send sputum for culture before antibiotics: it identifies the organism and guides the choice. Immunoglobulins and the sweat test look for a cause, not the organism.

steps.x: Which test, before antibiotics, in an exacerbation.
A community exacerbation; the key is to know the organism.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Sputum culture** to guide antibiotic choice.

elim: Too invasive for a mild exacerbation.
Not routine when well; does not identify the organism.
Looks for a cause of bronchiectasis, not the organism.
Tests for CF, not infection.

steps.x: **D. Sputum culture.**

practice.stem: A 35 year old man has newly diagnosed bronchiectasis on HRCT. He has had two pneumonias, recurrent sinusitis and an episode of giardiasis in the last 5 years. He has never smoked and has no gut symptoms between infections.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to identify the underlying cause?
practice.e: Recurrent sinopulmonary and gut infections with a low globulin suggest antibody deficiency (e.g. CVID): check serum immunoglobulins. The sweat test is for suspected CF.

steps.x: The diagnosis is made; you need the test for the **cause**.
Many different infections and a low globulin: immunodeficiency.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Serum immunoglobulins**.

elim: Bronchoscopy does not test immunity.
HRCT has already made the diagnosis.
Culture finds the organism, not the cause.
No pancreatic features or young age to suggest CF.

steps.x: **C. Serum immunoglobulins.**

practice.stem: A 45 year old woman has just been diagnosed with bronchiectasis on HRCT after years of a productive cough. She is otherwise well and is not currently having an exacerbation. Her sputum grows no Pseudomonas. She asks what she can do every day to help.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Chest physiotherapy with airway clearance techniques
practice.e: Chest physiotherapy (postural drainage, airway clearance) is first-line for stable bronchiectasis. Prophylactic azithromycin is reserved for 3 or more exacerbations a year.

steps.x: Initial management of stable disease.
New, stable, needs daily care.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Chest physiotherapy** with airway clearance.

elim: Inhaled steroids are not routine in bronchiectasis.
Only after 3 or more exacerbations a year.
No hypoxia mentioned.
Only if disease is confined to one lobe and other care fails.

steps.x: **A. Chest physiotherapy.**

practice.stem: A 57 year old man with bronchiectasis has 3 days of increased purulent sputum. A sample sent last month grew Pseudomonas aeruginosa. He has no allergies. His temperature is 37.5°C, pulse rate 90 bpm, BP 130/82 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 95% breathing air. He is managing at home.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate antibiotic management?
practice.e: A community bronchiectasis exacerbation is treated for 14 days; ciprofloxacin is the oral antibiotic that covers Pseudomonas. Five-day courses are for chest infections without bronchiectasis.

steps.x: Which antibiotic, for how long.
Community exacerbation, not septic, known Pseudomonas.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **14 days of oral ciprofloxacin**.

elim: Amoxicillin does not cover Pseudomonas, and 5 days is too short.
Clarithromycin does not cover Pseudomonas.
Doxycycline does not cover Pseudomonas.
Steroids do not treat an infective exacerbation.

steps.x: **B. Oral ciprofloxacin for 14 days.** Rule: bronchiectasis exacerbations get 14 days.

practice.stem: A 62 year old woman with bronchiectasis has had four exacerbations needing antibiotics in the last 12 months, despite twice-daily airway clearance physiotherapy and hypertonic saline. Her sputum repeatedly grows Haemophilus influenzae; Pseudomonas has never been isolated. Her ECG shows a normal QT interval.

visual.title: Exacerbations in 12 months
visual.caption: Four exacerbations despite optimal airway clearance.

practice.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
practice.e: Three or more exacerbations a year despite optimal management is the threshold for prophylactic antibiotics; without Pseudomonas, a long-term oral macrolide such as azithromycin is used.

steps.x: Next step after failure of first-line care.
Above the threshold of 3; no Pseudomonas; QT checked before a macrolide.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Prophylactic oral macrolide**: azithromycin.

elim: No hypoxia given.
Not a bronchiectasis treatment unless ABPA.
Steroids would increase infection risk.
No HRCT evidence of single-lobe disease.

steps.x: **C. Long-term oral azithromycin.** Rule: ≥3 a year = prophylaxis.

practice.stem: A 50 year old woman has had bronchiectasis since a severe pneumonia in childhood. HRCT shows bronchi wider than their accompanying arteries. Her sputum contains many neutrophils. She asks why her airways will not go back to normal even when the infections are treated.
practice.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of the irreversible airway dilatation?
o: Mucous gland hyperplasia narrowing the lumen
Proteases digesting elastin and cartilage in the bronchial wall
practice.e: Chronic neutrophilic inflammation releases proteases (e.g. elastase) that destroy the elastin and cartilage supporting the bronchial wall, so the dilatation is permanent.

steps.x: Mechanism of the permanent dilatation.

clues: bronchi wider than their accompanying arteries
will not go back to normal
steps.x: Signet ring sign; neutrophils release proteases; irreversible.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Proteases** destroy the wall's elastin and cartilage.

elim: Smooth muscle hypertrophy narrows airways (asthma).
Gland hyperplasia is chronic bronchitis and narrows, not widens.
Traction bronchiectasis occurs in fibrosis, not post-infective disease.
Type I hypersensitivity is asthma and reversible.

steps.x: **C. Proteases digesting elastin and cartilage.**
